technique: the exit — leaving on an image instead of a statement
lesson:
Today we work on one thing: the exit. The exit means the poem ends on a picture of something you can see, not on a sentence that explains or sums up.

Watch the last pictures this poem gives you. It shows "the day stands at the edge of the yard." It shows the day "shaking the wet from its coat." It shows "the kettle, the window, the small warm tasks." These are things with shape. You can picture each one.

This works because a picture stays in your head longer than a statement does. Your mind holds the kettle and the window after the words stop. You finish the poem looking at something, not thinking about a lesson.

Try this: write your last line as one object a person could point at. No explaining after it.

The second time through, listen for how the poem saves its one plain command, "So — up!", for after all those pictures.

Here is the poem.
poem:
The fog lets go of the low field slow,
unhooking from the stubble one row at a time,
and where it thins the hills come back to you,
brown-shouldered, patient, holding their own weather.
Wind turns the maples inside out, pale underleaf
flashing like fish before the rain decides.
It won't come yet. The air just leans that way,
heavy and sweet with the rot of fallen fruit.
A door bangs somewhere, loose on its latch,
and the day stands at the edge of the yard,
unhurried, unbothered, shaking the wet from its coat,
waiting on you to say the first word to it.

The kettle, the window, the small warm tasks that only wait for hands like yours —
they're ready whenever you are.

So — up!
